CRA Evidence Desk

Match your SBOM against an advisory export, see exactly which components are named, and download a dated record plus an Article 14 review draft. Nothing leaves your device — your SBOM is never uploaded.

Article 14's reporting duty starts 11 September 2026 — for products already on the EU market, not only new releases. This page does not tell you whether it applies to you; it helps you find the matches and draft the notification quickly once you decide it does.

1. Your files

2. Your product

Choose an SBOM and an advisory export, or try the example.

Findings

ComponentEcosystemAdvisorySummarySource

Not evaluated by this tool

These advisories stated their affected versions as a range. This tool matches exact versions and does not resolve ranges, so it has neither cleared nor flagged them — review each one yourself.

    Article 14 review draft

    
    
    
      
      Download draft (.txt)
      Download record (.json)
    
    
  
    

  
    What this does not check
    
  
      
    
    • Version ranges. An advisory saying "below 1.4.2" is reported as not evaluated, never resolved.
      • 
    
    • Reachability and exploitability. A matched component may not be reachable in your build at all.
      • 
    
    • Aliases and renames. A package published under two names matches only under the one your SBOM states.
      • 
    
    • Advisories you did not export. Coverage is exactly the file you supplied, on the day you ran it.
      • 
    
    • Whether an obligation applies. Severity, actively-exploited status and reporting deadlines are yours to determine.
      • 
  
    
  
    Review every finding against the authoritative advisory with a qualified professional before you rely on it.
    

  
    Questions
    
  
    When do CRA Article 14 reporting obligations start?
    
  
    
    11 September 2026, under Article 14(1) and (3): a manufacturer that
    becomes aware of an actively exploited vulnerability or a severe incident
    in a product with digital elements already on the EU market must notify
    ENISA — an early warning within 24 hours, a fuller notification within 72
    hours, and a final report within 14 days (actively exploited
    vulnerability) or one month (severe incident) after the 72-hour
    notification. It applies to products already on the market, not only new
    releases. This tool does not determine whether an obligation applies to
    your situation; it helps you find the matching components and draft the
    notification once you or a qualified professional decide it does.
  
    
  
    What SBOM formats does this accept?
    
  
    
    CycloneDX JSON (what npm sbom, syft, cdxgen and trivy emit),
    SPDX JSON, and a plain component list of the form
    {"components": [{"ecosystem", "name", "version"}]}. Package
    URLs are read where present, so an npm scope, a Maven group and a Go module
    path all resolve to the coordinates an advisory names them by. Nested
    CycloneDX sub-components are walked too.
  
    
  
    Why does it only match exact versions?
    
  
    
    Because resolving a version range is a judgement about your product, not a
    lookup. An advisory saying "all versions below 1.4.2" requires deciding how
    your ecosystem orders versions, whether a backport applies, and whether the
    vulnerable path is reachable in your build. This tool refuses to make that
    call on your behalf and instead names every range-only advisory in the
    report so you review it yourself. That refusal is the point: an exact match
    is evidence, an inferred one is an opinion.
  
    
  
    Does a match mean I have to file a CRA notification?
    
  
    
    No. A match means one component in your SBOM has the same name, ecosystem
    and version as an entry in the advisory export you supplied. Whether it is
    exploitable in your product, whether it is an actively exploited
    vulnerability or a severe incident under Article 14, and whether a
    reporting deadline applies are all determinations for you and a qualified
    professional. The tool produces a draft to review, never a filing.
  
    
  
    Is my SBOM uploaded anywhere?
    
  
    
    No. The files are read by your own browser and nothing is transmitted.
    There is no server, no account, and no upload step — you can disconnect
    from the network and the tool still works. This matters more than usual
    here: an SBOM is a complete map of your product's dependencies, and an
    advisory match list is a map of its exposure.
  
    
  
    What does a clean report actually prove?
    
  
    
    Only that no component in the SBOM you supplied exactly matched an entry in
    the advisory export you supplied, on the day you ran it. It is not a
    vulnerability scan, not conformity assessment, and not coverage of
    advisories you did not export. If part of your export stated versions as
    ranges, the report says so explicitly, because a clean result read without
    that caveat would look like far more assurance than it is.
  
    
  
    My SBOM and my advisory export spell packages differently. Now what?
    
  
    
    That is the normal case, not a broken export — the two formats name the
    same registry two ways, and this tool folds them onto one spelling before
    matching. Why
    don't my SBOM and advisory package names match? walks through where
    the mismatches come from and which ones can be resolved without guessing.
  
    
  
    How is this different from OWASP Dependency-Track?
    
  
    
    Dependency-Track is a continuous, self-hosted SBOM-analysis server; this
    is a free, one-shot page with nothing to deploy. See
    CRA Evidence Desk vs. OWASP
    Dependency-Track for the full comparison.
  
    
  
    Can't I just match my SBOM to the advisory list by eye?
    
  
    
    For a handful of components, yes. It stops being reliable once ecosystem
    names are spelled two different ways across the two files, a component is
    nested rather than top-level, or an advisory names a version range instead
    of a list. See
    CRA Evidence Desk vs. matching an SBOM
    to advisories by hand for where a manual read breaks down.
  
    

  
    
    
    Disclaimer
    
    
    
      No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is,
      without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal,
      regulatory, or compliance advice, and it does not replace a qualified
      professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its
      output before relying on it, and for meeting any obligation it
      helps you prepare for. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the
      authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.
    
    
    
    
      Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free,
      experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without
      notice. Do not use this page as a system of record — if a draft needs to
      survive, download it.
    
    

    
    Privacy
    
    
    
      Everything runs in your browser. Your SBOM is never uploaded, and we
      don't have accounts, tracking cookies, or an analytics vendor. This page
      counts anonymous, local feature-use events (e.g. "a match was run") in
      your own browser's localStorage — never component names,
      advisory ids, filenames, or anything identifying — only to help this
      project's maintainers tell whether the tool is used at all. Nothing is
      sent anywhere.
      
      
    
    

    
    
      There is a command-line version of this tool in the same repository if
      you would rather run it in CI: it reads the same formats and prints the
      same draft.
    
    

    
    
      Also tracking which third-party access changed at a customer? The
      Shopify permission drift record
      compares two app-scope exports and shows exactly what changed —
      nothing uploaded.

sbom-and-advisory-package-names-dont-mat.text:
Why don't my SBOM and advisory package names match?

Short answer: both files are correct, and they are describing the same package in two different spellings. An exact-match comparison takes each at its word, so the mismatch is real until one spelling is folded onto the other.

Where the mismatches come from

Three places, in roughly the order they bite:

  1. The registry is named differently. A package URL carries a purl type; an OSV advisory carries an ecosystem name. For several registries those are two strings for one place.
  2. Maven punctuates differently. A purl splits the coordinate into namespace and name; OSV writes group:artifact.
  3. OSV adds a distribution qualifier. An ecosystem can arrive as Alpine:v3.19 where the SBOM simply says alpine.

None of these are visible as errors in either file, which is why a hand-rolled comparison tends to report a confident, wrong zero.

The registries that are spelled two ways

Five, and only five, of the registries this tool reads are named differently by the two formats:

OSV ecosystempurl type
crates.iocargo
Gogolang
Packagistcomposer
RubyGemsgem
SwiftURLswift

Everything else in the table this tool reads — npm, PyPI, Maven, NuGet, Hex, Pub, CRAN, Hackage — already agrees between the two, once case is set aside. Where the two disagree, the purl spelling wins, because purl is the identifier the SBOM formats themselves carry.

Questions

Why doesn't my SBOM's package name match the advisory's?

Because the two files use different naming conventions for the same registry, and an exact-match comparison takes them at their word. A CycloneDX or SPDX SBOM carries package URLs, whose type is the registry's purl spelling. An OSV advisory carries an ecosystem name instead, and for several registries that is a different string for the same place: golang against Go, cargo against crates.io, packagist against composer, rubygems against gem. Nothing is wrong with either file. They simply never meet until one spelling is folded onto the other.

Why do Maven packages fail when every other ecosystem works?

Maven is the one ecosystem where the two conventions disagree about punctuation rather than about a registry's name. A package URL splits a Maven coordinate into a namespace and a name, while OSV writes the same coordinate as group colon artifact. Every other ecosystem in this table joins with a slash, because that is what its names look like in the wild: an npm scope reads at-scope slash name, a Go module path reads github.com slash owner slash repo. So joining a Maven coordinate the same way produces a name that is correctly assembled and still matches nothing.

What is a package URL, and why prefer it as the canonical spelling?

A package URL, usually written purl, states a registry, a name and a version in one string. It is the identifier the SBOM formats themselves carry, which is why it is used as the canonical spelling wherever the two inputs disagree. Its qualifiers and subpath are dropped before matching: an architecture or a subdirectory narrows which build is being described, not which package is named, so carrying them into the comparison would only invent mismatches.

Why does my advisory export say Alpine colon v3.19 when my SBOM just says alpine?

OSV qualifies some ecosystems with a distribution release. The qualifier narrows which advisories apply, not which package is named, so it is dropped at the colon before matching. Keeping it would mean a plain alpine in an SBOM could never match an advisory for the release that SBOM was built from, which is the opposite of what the qualifier is there to express.

If names are normalised, is the tool guessing at matches?

No, and the distinction is the whole coverage boundary. Folding two spellings of the same registry onto one is reading what both files already state. Inferring is deciding something neither file says. This tool does the first and never the second: it does not resolve aliases, affected version ranges, reachability, or exploitability. An advisory that expresses affected versions only as a range therefore contributes no match at all, and is reported as not evaluated rather than dropped, because a clean result means something very different when part of the export was never assessed.

One entry in my SBOM is malformed. Is the whole file rejected?

No. A package URL that cannot be parsed is skipped rather than raised, and that component's own name, ecosystem and version fields are read instead. A single bad entry among two thousand good ones should not cost you the file, and a component that states usable coordinates some other way is still matched on those.

Want the comparison done for you? CRA Evidence Desk folds both spellings onto one, matches your SBOM against your advisory export on exact name, ecosystem and version, and names the advisories it could not evaluate. It runs entirely in your browser, your SBOM is never uploaded, and it is free.

It is general technical explanation of how two file formats name packages — not legal, regulatory, or compliance advice, and not a determination that any obligation does or does not apply to you. Naming conventions change, and an export from a tool not described here may differ. You are responsible for verifying any match against the authoritative advisory source before relying on it. vs-dependency-track.html.text:
← CRA Evidence Desk

CRA Evidence Desk vs. OWASP Dependency-Track

Two different shapes: Dependency-Track is a continuous, self-hosted SBOM-analysis server you run and maintain. This is a free, one-shot page or CLI for a single question — do this SBOM and this advisory export name any of the same components right now, and can I get a reviewable Article 14 draft out of that in minutes.

What each tool is for

OWASP Dependency-Track is a free, open-source platform that organizations deploy as a running service (Docker containers plus a database) to ingest SBOMs continuously and watch every tracked component — libraries, containers, operating systems, firmware, services — against multiple vulnerability-intelligence sources (the NVD, Sonatype OSS Index, GitHub Advisories, OSV, and others) for as long as it keeps running, so a CVE disclosed after your last build still fires an alert. It has a policy engine, EPSS-based prioritisation, and portfolio-wide project tracking. Running it is an ongoing operational commitment: someone has to deploy it, secure the database and API, patch it, and keep it fed.

CRA Evidence Desk does none of that. It has no server, no database, and no memory between visits — it is a static page (or a CLI you run by hand or in CI) that reads one SBOM and one advisory export you already have and makes only exact name/ecosystem/version matches, names the advisories it could not evaluate, and exports a dated JSON record plus a customer-reviewed Article 14 notification draft. It does not watch anything over time, does not carry its own vulnerability database, and needs nothing installed or kept running.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I want continuous monitoring across every project I ship, watching new advisories as they are published, with a policy engine and prioritisation.Dependency-Track — that ongoing, portfolio-wide watch is what it is built for.
I have one SBOM and one advisory export in hand right now and need to know which named components actually match, plus a draft I can hand a reviewer today.CRA Evidence Desk — free, instant, private, nothing to deploy.
I don't want to stand up, secure, and patch a server just to answer one reporting question.CRA Evidence Desk — it is a static page or a single CLI invocation, not a service.
I need a document shaped for a specific obligation — a CRA Article 14 notification draft — not a general vulnerability dashboard.CRA Evidence Desk's draft output is built around that one document.
I want my own private vulnerability-intelligence database, aggregated from multiple public feeds, kept current automatically.Dependency-Track — it maintains that database for you as a running service.
Does the tool upload my SBOM anywhere?CRA Evidence Desk: no, it never leaves your device. Dependency-Track: it is designed to receive SBOMs, since ingesting and storing them is its job.

Most vendors get different value from each: Dependency-Track (or a comparable SCA platform) for an always-on watch across a whole portfolio, and a tool like this one for an instant, no-deployment check of one SBOM against one advisory export before a specific filing question. This page's own output is a single evidence artifact from the inputs you gave it, not a vulnerability database, a continuous scan, or a substitute for reviewing the advisories yourself.

This tool needs no install and no server: it is a static page, the matching runs in your browser (or as a single CLI command), and once loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use CRA Evidence Desk or OWASP Dependency-Track?

They solve different problems. Dependency-Track is a continuous SBOM-analysis server: you deploy it (Docker containers, a database, ongoing patching and access control), feed it SBOMs over time, and it watches every component against multiple vulnerability-intelligence sources for as long as it keeps running, with a policy engine and EPSS-based prioritisation across your whole portfolio of projects. CRA Evidence Desk does none of that. It is a static page or a CLI, not a server: give it one CycloneDX/SPDX SBOM and one advisory export (OSV or a plain list) and it makes only exact name, ecosystem and version matches, names what it could not evaluate, and produces a dated JSON record plus an Article 14 draft. Nothing is installed, nothing runs between visits, and nothing is uploaded. A vendor already running Dependency-Track gets continuous monitoring from the platform it operates; a vendor who needs a single, disclosed evidence artifact right now, or who does not want to stand up and secure a server to get one, is in the right place here.

Is this page affiliated with OWASP or Dependency-Track?

No. This page is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by the OWASP Foundation or the Dependency-Track project. Dependency-Track is free, open-source software; it is named here only to describe what this tool is and is not.

Open the CRA Evidence Desk to run your own SBOM and advisory export, or see why your SBOM and advisory package names don't match first if the two files use different spellings for the same registry.

vs-matching-by-hand.html.text:
← CRA Evidence Desk

CRA Evidence Desk vs. matching an SBOM to advisories by hand

Reading a CycloneDX export and an OSV advisory list side by side and noting the overlaps is a generic manual habit anyone with the two files already has, not a company or product this could be mistaken for. It works for a handful of components and breaks down well before a real dependency tree's size does.

Where the manual read breaks down

Matching two lists by eye is really computing an exact set intersection, and a person does that slower and less reliably than a matcher that runs the same rule on every entry. Three specific gaps matter more than the general slowness:

CaseMatching by handThis tool
Same registry, spelled differently (golang vs. Go, cargo vs. crates.io, Maven namespace/name vs. group:artifact)A real match reads as no match unless the reviewer already knows every spelling pair and normalizes them while scanningFolds both spellings onto one form before comparing, using package URLs wherever present
Sub-components nested inside a parent in a CycloneDX SBOMA read that only walks the top-level dependency list never reaches themWalks nested sub-components the same as top-level ones
An advisory stated as a version range rather than an enumerated listRequires an on-the-spot judgment call about that ecosystem's version ordering to accept or rejectDoes not guess a range; lists it under advisories not evaluated rather than silently dropping it
A record of what was checked and whenRarely survives past the review sessionExports a dated JSON record every run
Hundreds of components against hundreds of advisoriesAttention and consistency both degrade well before the end of the listApplies the identical exact-match rule to every entry, first to last

None of this makes the manual read useless -- for two or three components a quick look is often faster than exporting files into a tool. The gap opens as the SBOM and the advisory export grow, which is exactly when a manual reviewer is least likely to notice they have started missing things.

This tool needs no install and no server: it is a static page, the matching runs in your browser (or as a single CLI command), and once loaded it keeps working with the connection off. Nothing you give it is uploaded.

Common questions

Isn't comparing two lists something I can just do by eye?

For a handful of components, yes -- scan the SBOM's package names, scan the advisory list, note the overlaps. It stops being reliable once a CycloneDX export runs to hundreds of nested sub-components and an OSV advisory export runs to hundreds of entries, because the task is not really reading two lists, it is computing an exact set intersection across two large lists that do not always spell the same thing the same way. That is a mechanical task a person does slower and less consistently than a matcher that never gets tired partway through.

What actually goes wrong when someone matches by hand?

The most common miss is an ecosystem-naming mismatch: a CycloneDX SBOM and an OSV advisory can name the same registry two different ways -- golang vs. Go, cargo vs. crates.io -- and a Maven artifact as namespace/name in one export and group:artifact in the other. A component and its advisory that genuinely match will not visibly match on a side-by-side read unless the reviewer already knows every one of those spelling pairs and normalizes them in their head while scanning. The second common miss is nested components: CycloneDX SBOMs can nest sub-components inside a parent, and a manual read that only walks the top-level dependency list never reaches them.

What about an advisory that names a version range instead of a list?

OSV advisories state affected versions two ways: an enumerated list, or a range such as "everything below 1.4.2." A manual reviewer looking at a range has to decide on the spot whether their installed version falls inside it, which means knowing that ecosystem's own version-ordering rules and whether a backport changes the answer -- a judgment call about the product, not a lookup. Treating a range as a quick yes-or-no during a fast manual pass is exactly where a wrong call costs the most, because the advisory that gets waved through is the one that actually matched.

Does a clean manual read leave any record of what was checked?

Usually not one that survives past the meeting. A person who reads through an SBOM and an advisory export and concludes nothing matches rarely writes down which advisories they evaluated, which they skipped because they only stated a range, or the date they looked. Six months later, when a reporting question comes up, nothing says what was actually checked. This tool exports a dated JSON record every time, and lists advisories it could not evaluate by name rather than silently dropping them, so the same question later has an answer instead of a memory.

Does this tool replace judgment about whether a match matters?

No. It only makes exact name, ecosystem, and version matches and tells you which advisories it could not evaluate. It does not resolve aliases, ranges, reachability, or exploitability, and it does not decide whether a legal reporting obligation applies to a given match. What it replaces is the mechanical part -- comparing two lists exactly, the same way, every time -- not the judgment calls that come after a match is found.

Open CRA Evidence Desk to run your own SBOM and advisory export, or see why your SBOM and advisory package names don't match for the ecosystem-spelling gap in more detail, or CRA Evidence Desk vs. OWASP Dependency-Track if you are weighing this against a continuous monitoring platform instead of a manual read.
